newsitem.title: UK: Sleaze beats Europe as British election issue.
newsitem.headline: Sleaze beats Europe as British election issue.

text.p: It was the single most potent issue, the "clear blue water" in political jargon that would separate Britain's ruling party from the opposition.
Europe, senior Conservatives told Prime Minister John Major, was the issue to bring voters to their senses and return the ruling party to power.
Once the looming threat of a federal European superstate -- and Labour's willingness to go along with it -- was clear, back would flock the voters, confounding the pollsters as in 1992.
But the May 1 election is approaching fast and Europe is yet to make its mark on the campaign, partly due to Labour's safety first strategy towards ending 18 years in opposition.

The party's modernising leader Tony Blair adroitly steered Labour's European policy towards the Conservatives and dropped anchor alongside, effectively challenging Major to sail even further to the right if he wanted to open up "clear blue water".
Major offered a referendum before joining a single European currency? So would Labour, said Blair.
Major said it was unlikely Britain would join a European single currency in 1999. Labour's manifesto stressed the "formidable obstacles" to British entry when it starts.

Polls show Blair's manoeuvering has worked -- at least on Europe. A poll for Reuters by NOP this week showed 33 percent of voters trust Labour most to manage Britain's relations with Europe. Just 29 percent trust the Conservatives most.

Major's problem is that his party's European policy has been bedevilled by arguments and rebellions for years, sabotaging any claims he makes to represent a party which speaks with one voice on relations with the European Union.

Labour has pledged to sign up for the social chapter which sets out standards for worker protection across the 15-nation bloc. Major argues this, and Labour's promise of a -- as yet unspecified -- minimum wage will hit jobs.
But Labour has countered this with plans for a drive to get the young and long-term unemployed back to work financed by a "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utilities.

Left without a clear target -- a tactic public relations experts see as central to Labour's campaign strategy -- Major and his ministers have been forced to fall back on warnings that Europe is encroaching on Britain's sovereignty.
But Major's problem is that this does not go far enough to satisfy strident anti-Europeans.

Caught in a clinch between the Referendum Party, set up by entrepreneur James Goldsmith to demand looser links with Europe, taking votes off the Conservatives on the right and Labour in the centre, Major has been left with little room for manoeuvre.

Labour cut this even further last weekend. Foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook told a television interviewer: "If you didn't join (a European single currency) in 1999, it is unlikely you would be joining in the course of the next parliament."

The apparent shift to an even harder line increased pressure on Major to rule out entry in the next parliament whatever happens. Major has so far resisted, perhaps wary of the reaction from pro-Europeans like finance minister Kenneth Clarke.
But, with the Conservatives shorn of a distinctive policy on Europe to set it apart from Labour, it is hardly surprising that media and voters are focusing instead on allegations of corruption.
The NOP poll showed 18 percent of voters believe sleaze will have a big effect on the outcome of the election.
